script: [serious] The story goes like this. In October 1943, at the Philadelphia Navy Yard, the United States Navy switched on a machine. A warship, the destroyer escort U.S.S. Eldridge, was wrapped in a strange green fog. And then it was gone. Not hidden. Gone. According to the legend, the ship reappeared more than two hundred miles away, in Norfolk, Virginia, where sailors on another ship watched it sit in the harbor for a few minutes before it vanished again and returned to Philadelphia. The crew, the story says, came back changed. Some were fused into the steel of the deck. Some went mad. Some kept fading in and out of sight for years. It has been called the Navy's darkest secret. It has inspired books, films and decades of late-night radio. Millions of people have heard some version of it. But almost nobody has heard where it actually came from. Because when you follow the paper trail, the Philadelphia Experiment doesn't start with a scientist or a sailor. It starts with a man writing letters. This is the story of how one man's letters turned into one of the most famous military legends in history, and what the Navy's own records say really happened. In 1955, a writer named Morris Jessup published a book called The Case for the UFO. His book speculated about how flying saucers might move. In January 1956, he started getting letters. They were signed Carlos Miguel Allende. The writer claimed he had been a merchant sailor during the war, aboard a ship called the S.S. Andrew Furuseth. And he said he had seen something impossible. He described the Navy using unpublished theories of Albert Einstein to make a warship invisible, and he named a scientist, Franklin Reno, who he said had made it work. The letters were rambling, oddly capitalized and full of strange spellings. But they were specific. A ship. A place. A date. Jessup wrote back and asked for proof. The answer he got was strange. Allende said he could not remember the details clearly, and that his memory would have to be recovered first. He pointed Jessup to a Philadelphia newspaper story about sailors in a bar fight who vanished in front of witnesses. That article has never been found. Carlos Miguel Allende, it turned out, did not exist either. His real name was Carl Meredith Allen. Before the letters even started, something else had arrived in Washington. In late 1955, the Office of Naval Research received an anonymous package. It was marked Happy Easter. Inside was a copy of Jessup's book. Its margins were covered in handwritten notes, in three different shades of blue ink, apparently from three different people, one of them calling himself Jemi. The notes talked about invisibility, force fields and the experiment in Philadelphia, as if the writers knew all about it. In 1957, Jessup was invited to the Office of Naval Research to look at it. He recognized the handwriting at once. It matched the letters from Allende. Two officers there, Captain Sidney Sherby and Commander George Hoover, were curious enough to share the annotated book with a defense contractor, Varo Manufacturing, in Garland, Texas. Varo made copies. About a dozen at first, eventually a hundred and twenty-seven. They became known as the Varo edition. Commander Hoover later said he found nothing of substance in the invisibility claims. But that didn't matter. A strange book had passed through the hands of naval officers and been copied by a military contractor. To believers, that looked like proof the Navy was worried. In 1959, Jessup died. The legend kept going without him. For the next twenty years, the story spread the way legends do. In 1965, an author named Vincent Gaddis retold it in a book about mysteries of the sea, using the notes from the Varo edition. In 1979, Charles Berlitz, already famous for writing about the Bermuda Triangle, published The Philadelphia Experiment, Project Invisibility, with co-author William Moore. It was presented as fact. Critics pointed out that key details looked very similar to a thriller novel published the year before. In 1984, Hollywood made a film. It turned the story into a time-travel adventure, and it was loosely based on the accounts at best. Then, starting in 1989, a man named Al Bielek began telling audiences that he had been aboard the Eldridge during the experiment. At a UFO conference, he said the movie was largely consistent with what he had seen. Notice what happened here. Every retelling added something. A green fog. Teleportation. Time travel. Sailors trapped in the deck. And every new detail made the story feel more real, because it had more people telling it. But not one of those new details came from a document. They came from books, a novel and a movie. So what do the documents actually say? Start with the ship itself. The U.S.S. Eldridge was commissioned in August 1943, in New York. According to the Navy's own summary of her war diary, in October 1943 she was nowhere near Philadelphia. She was near Bermuda until October fifteenth. Then she sailed in a convoy to New York, arriving on October eighteenth, and stayed in New York harbor until November first. What about Allen's ship, the Andrew Furuseth? Its movement records show it arriving off Cape Henry, near Norfolk, on October fourth, after a round trip to Casablanca, and leaving Norfolk in a convoy on October twenty-fifth, a week before the Eldridge ever got there. Its captain wrote a letter flatly denying that he or his crew saw anything unusual while in Norfolk. Decades later, veterans of the Eldridge held a reunion and told a Philadelphia newspaper their ship had never even made port in Philadelphia. And the scientific claim? The Navy says making a ship invisible with force fields does not conform to known physical laws. Einstein's unified field theory, the one the legend depends on, was never completed. Einstein did work for the Navy during the war, as a part-time consultant to the Bureau of Ordnance. His subject was explosives. Not invisibility. And the Office of Naval Research, the agency at the center of the story, said in 1996 that it had never researched radar invisibility, in 1943 or at any other time. It didn't even exist until 1946. So was anything real? Probably, yes. Just not what the legend says. During the war, the Navy was fighting a deadly threat, German magnetic mines that exploded when a steel hull passed over them. The answer was a process called degaussing. Electrical cables were wrapped around a ship's hull to cancel out its magnetic field, making it effectively invisible, but only to a mine. A degaussed ship was still visible to the eye, to radar and to sonar. Researcher Jacques Vallée traced the story to degaussing work on another destroyer escort, the U.S.S. Engstrom, and even found a veteran who said he had been one of the sailors in the famous bar story, and that nobody vanished at all. Secret magnetic work, a few sailors' stories, and the legend had its seed. As for Carl Allen, he later said he had written the notes in Jessup's book himself, to scare him. A family member described him to a local reporter as a master leg-puller. So here is what the file tells us. The Philadelphia Experiment is not really a story about a ship. It's a story about how a legend is built. One man's letters. A book that passed through a government office. Officers who were curious, not alarmed. And then decades of writers, each adding a little more. The scariest part isn't the green fog. It's how easily a few letters became history. Do you think there's anything more to it? Tell me in the comments. This is Dossier Decoded.
